newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament approves new bank privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament approves new bank privatisation law.

text.p: Slovak parliament on Wednesday approved a new privatisation law effectively allowing the selloff of state stakes in two major banks, but only after a last minute concession by opposition deputies.

Parliament approved the measure, which replaced a draft halting the sale of four financial institutions until 2003, after the opposition accepted a government plan to leave the two largest -- insurer Slovenska Poistovna and savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna -- untouched.
The measure thus allows two other major commerical banks, IRB and VUB, to be privatised.
"We gave political guarantees to the ZRS (Workers' Party) that Sporitelna and Poistovna will not be privatised until the end of this term," Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik told parliament.
The law was then approved by a large majority, with 124 of the deputies present voting in favour, three against, and 12 abstentions. Four deputies did not vote at all.

Through the state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund, the state controls 91.3 percent of Slovenska Sporitelna, 50.5 percent Slovenska Poistovna, some 35 percent in IRB and about 51.49 percent in VUB.
The original law suspending bank privatisation was approved last month after the ultra-left ZRS, a junior partner in the ruling coalition, crossed the floor to vote in tandem with the opposition.
The government, however, then asked President Michal Kovac to return the law for re-assessment, which he promptly did.

The opposition approved the original law because it wanted the banks to be restructured before selling the state's stake, and feared many of the shares would end up in hands of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's allies.

But opposition deputies said they voted for the proposal since it was the least unacceptable option of those they faced after a proposal on the compromise solution narrowly gained approval earlier in the day's session.
"We have chosen the lesser of two evils by approving the measure in its second version," said Ludovit Cermak of the opposition Democratic Union.
Kozlik said the government has a restructuring plan for the banks, but that it expects money to finance the plan to come from revenues generated by the banks' privatisation.
The move should help boost Slovakia's chances for gaining membership into the Organisation of Economic

The OECD has said that while no one issue determines whether a country is accepted to the group, Slovakia must show it is committed to free market principles, and the extent to which effective market access is possible for foreign direct investors -- including the privatisation of state-owned assets.

"...many OECD representatives have expressed concern over the (original) law saying it will make a number of complications for Slovak membership in the OECD," Kozlik explained to parliament as to why the amendment was needed.
Of the former Soviet satellites, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland have already joined the club of advanced nations.

But Slovakia, afflicted by political turmoil in recent years, has yet to gain membership although it was once considered to be in the vanguard of post-communist countries seeking to join western institutions.
